title: Copy List with Random Pointer
category: Linked List · Hash map of copies
summary: Deep-copy a list where each node also has a `random` pointer to any node (or null). First pass: create a copy of every node and map original → copy. Second pass: set each copy's `next` and `random` by looking up the originals' targets in the map.

complexity.note: The interleaving trick brings space to O(1).

intuition: A random pointer may point forward, so copies must exist before wiring.
The map translates any original node into its copy.
`map.get(null)` returns null, which handles null pointers for free.
pitfalls: Pointing a copy's random at the original node.
Trying to wire random pointers in a single pass before their targets exist.

title: Decode String
summary: Decode strings like "3[a2[c]]" into "accaccacc". Use two stacks: on '[', push the current repeat count and the text built so far, then start fresh. On ']', pop them and append the inner text repeated that many times.

complexity.note: The output can be much longer than the input.

intuition: Brackets nest, so the innermost group must finish first: a stack.
Numbers can have several digits: `k = k * 10 + digit`.
On ']', the text built inside the brackets is repeated and attached to the outer text.
pitfalls: String concatenation in loops is slow; use StringBuilder.

title: Find the Duplicate Number
category: Fast and slow pointers · Cycle in an array
summary: n + 1 numbers in the range 1..n, exactly one value repeated; find it without modifying the array and in O(1) space. Treat each value as a pointer `i → nums[i]`. The duplicate value is where two pointers lead into the same index, the entrance to a cycle. Floyd's tortoise and hare finds it.
intuition: Index 0 is never a target (values are 1..n), so it's a safe start outside the cycle.
Phase 1: slow moves 1 step, fast 2 steps, until they meet inside the cycle.
Phase 2: reset one pointer to 0; move both 1 step. They meet at the cycle entrance: the duplicate.
pitfalls: Sorting or marking negatives modifies the array, which is forbidden.

Python.code:
def findDuplicate(nums: List[int]) -> int:
    slow = fast = 0
    while True:
        slow = nums[slow]
        fast = nums[nums[fast]]
        if slow == fast: break
    slow = 0
    while slow != fast:
        slow = nums[slow]
        fast = nums[fast]
    return slow

title: Valid Sudoku
summary: Check that the filled cells of a 9×9 board break no rule: no repeated digit in any row, column, or 3×3 box. Scan every cell once and record keys like "5 in row 0", "5 in col 3", "5 in box 1" in a set; a failed insert means a repeat.
intuition: The box index of (r, c) is `(r / 3) * 3 + c / 3`.
One set of string keys covers all three rules.
Empty cells ('.') are ignored; the board doesn't need to be solvable.
pitfalls: Trying to check solvability; the problem only asks about the current cells.
Getting the box index formula wrong.

title: Basic Calculator II
summary: Evaluate an expression with + − × ÷ and spaces, respecting precedence. Read numbers left to right, remembering the operator before each one. + and − push the number (or its negative) on a stack; × and ÷ combine immediately with the stack's top. The answer is the stack's sum.

complexity.note: Can be done in O(1) space by keeping only the last term.

intuition: × and ÷ bind tighter, so apply them right away to the previous term.
+ and − are deferred: push signed terms and add them at the end.
Process the pending operator when you hit the next operator or the end of the string.
Division truncates toward zero.
pitfalls: Forgetting to process the last number.
Applying + immediately breaks precedence: "3+2*2" must be 7.

title: Sliding Window Maximum
summary: Return the maximum of every window of size k. Keep a deque of indices whose values are decreasing. Before adding index i, pop smaller values from the back (they can never be a maximum again) and drop the front if it slid out of the window. The front is always the current maximum.

complexity.note: Each index is pushed and popped at most once.

intuition: A value smaller than a newer value is useless: the newer one outlives it and beats it.
So the deque stays decreasing from front to back.
Store indices to know when the front leaves the window.
Record `nums[deque.front]` once the first full window is formed.
pitfalls: A max-heap works but is O(n log n) and needs lazy deletion.
Storing values instead of indices loses track of expiry.

title: First Missing Positive
summary: Find the smallest missing positive integer in O(n) time and O(1) space. The answer is in 1..n+1, so place each value v in 1..n at index v − 1 by swapping. Afterwards, the first index i with `nums[i] != i + 1` gives the answer i + 1.

complexity.note: Each swap puts one value in its final place, so at most n swaps.

intuition: Only values 1..n matter; anything else can be ignored.
Swap `nums[i]` to its home `nums[i] − 1` until the current slot holds a useless or already-placed value.
Check `nums[nums[i] − 1] != nums[i]` to avoid infinite swaps on duplicates.
If every slot is correct, the answer is n + 1.
pitfalls: Sorting is O(n log n); a HashSet is O(n) space.
